utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Cetina, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you have given at the beginning of your testimony. Ms. Mahindaratne, are you ready to continue your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Cetina.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Just two questions on the subject we were discussing last evening, you know, I showed you a document where you had sent a report of certain investigations carried out to General Cermak, and you couldn't recall why you had sent that document to him. Now, isn't it correct, Mr. Cetina, that if General Cermak asked you to carry out a specific task, let us say, for example, to carry out an investigation into a specific incident, you'd comply with that request, would you not?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he provided me with information, then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And once you had carried out that task that General Cermak had asked to you carry out, would you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could we be very careful in our language here, Your Honour, because there is a lot of heavy meaning within concern words, such as "tasks" and the issue here. And I notice the witness answer, "if he provided me with information," and we know the -- the police system of dealing with information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, Ms. Mahindaratne, you're -- let me -- let me try to rephrase your question and tell me, please, if you would think that the question would be different. Mr. Cetina, if Mr. Cermak would have asked you to carry out an investigation and if he would have given you the information you needed for that, and then, Ms. Mahindaratne, I take it that you wanted to ask the witness whether he would then report back to Mr. Cermak about the activities which Mr. Cetina would have developed as a result of being asked to investigate.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Exactly, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not advise him about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was not under an obligation of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, perhaps we could do it in a more factual way. Mr. Cetina, because some people even now and then do things, although there is no obligation to do so, would have you considered to, if being asked and if being provided with information to -- to investigate a matter, even without being obliged to do so, would you inform Mr. Cermak about the activities that you have -- you would have developed as a result of what he asked you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If he had asked me to inform him and if it was important to him, then, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the answer you earlier gave, that you would not advise him about, is an answer which would not apply to all circumstances. If you would know that it was important for him, and if you -- if he would have asked you to report back to him, then you would have done so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I can offer an explanation, with your leave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd rather first have an answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have informed him had he asked me to inform him. Otherwise, in principle, I would not have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, may I have document D595, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, this is a document that we -- that was discussed the day before yesterday in direct examination. Now, in your testimony, there was much discussion about co-operation of civilian police and military police in addressing crimes. And you testified that you attended a meeting in Plitvice - pardon my pronunciation if I didn't say it right - where the military police and the civilian police and senior officers of the Ministry of Interior met to discuss co-operation. Now, these are minutes of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if we could move the -- the first paragraph reads that -- recorded a meeting with representatives of RH MUP was held on 15th September, 1995, at 1100 hours. And the topic was: "Analysis of the tasks carried out in a newly liberated part of the Republic of Croatia during and after the Oluja/Storm operation."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you have -- the assistant minister, Mr. Moric, was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if you could just move to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There we have, in paragraph 1: "Mr. Moric opened the meeting with a short reference to 1991 and, having given an introduction to the meeting subject, he gave the floor to the heads of the police administrations, who, in their presentations, passed on the information on number of committed criminal acts and measures taken against perpetrators of the said, and also spoke about problems of jurisdiction of state attorney's offices in the local communities in joint solving ... the crimes." And then the same page, right at the bottom, is your own address that is noted. "Mr. Cetina, chief of the police administration for Zadar and Knin, put the emphasis on that fact that the biggest part of that area had been occupied. The situation in this area, he divided into three stages: Stage 1, stay of the HV professional units; Stage 2, stay of parts of the units which burnt houses and threatened with arms if tried to be prevented from committing crimes; Stage 3, stay of civilians which were taking property away on a massive scale."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if you could move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "He also assessed the co-operation with the military police as unsatisfactory, due to the insufficient number of military policemen." Now, Mr. Cetina, those three stages that you described, do you understand those three stages as three stages during which crimes were committed?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Stage 2 and Stage 3, clearly, indicate crimes. Can you tell us, Stage 1, was -- what was the period of duration of Stage 1, that is, the stay of professional units? What was the duration of time from the point of -- from the completion of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak in terms of days, because I do not remember many things.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was there a distinct separation of the stay of the professional units as opposed to at least -- let me put it this way: Was there a distinct separation from Stage 1 to Stage 2, or did they overlap?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my per perception that they overlapped.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, -- now, this Phase 2, Stage 2, you record a stay of parts of the units which "burnt houses and threatened with arms if tried to prevent from committing crimes." Now, yesterday, when Mr. Misetic questioned you, and I will take you to that -- this is in the draft transcript, page 5. Your question by

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Q. Mr. Cetina, do you agree with me that the police had the authority to detain members of the Croatian army at check-points, if, for example, they were found to have looted items in their possession. They were allowed to detain them and then they were supposed to call in the military police so that these individuals could be processed further in the military crime justice system?" And your answer was: "A. Yes, that's all right in theory. But in practice, things were different." And then, further through that examination, the Bench asked you some questions -- Presiding Judge asked you this question: "When Mr. Misetic gave you a picture of what could happen at a check-point, he asked whether that was how the system worked, and you said: 'I could agree. But in practice, it depended on the assessment of the police officers involved. They were supposed to estimate whether this could lead to a conflict.' "What kind of conflict were you referring to?" And your answer was: "A conflict in the sense that such people could resist being identified. We discussed that yesterday. We insisted that at check-points, together with our police officers, there be the military police as well." And further on, the Presiding Judge asked you, Witness: "You would say that if the civilian police would take action against such a person under those circumstances, that whether or not to do that would depend on their estimate on whether those persons would accept such an intervention by the civilian police in the absence of the military police. Is that how I have to understand your answer?" You said: "Precisely." Now, this second stage that you talk about where units were committing crimes and threatened with arms -- let me just see -- the stay of parts of the units which burnt houses and thereafter with arms tried to be prevented from committing crimes. Now, was that the type of conflict you were referring to yesterday?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that no HV members were ever identified by the police, but it's simply the way things were in the field, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, my question is this, Mr. Cetina. Now, in saying -- now yesterday you said, of course, in law the civilian police could detain a HV member but in practice it did not happen. And in response to the questions from the Bench you referred to the conflict. Now, my question to you is: Is this the type of conflict that you referred to, as a possible consequence, if civilian police attempted to intervene to stop crimes committed by military personnel in the absence of military police?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question, Mr. President. The witness did not state what Ms. Mahindaratne says he stated in the second sentence of her question that "in practice it did not happen."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me tell you exactly what you said Mr. Cetina. You said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you quote literally, then there will be no problem, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When Mr. Misetic put that suggestion to you, you said: "Yes, that's all right in theory, but in practice, things were different." And then further on you discuss a possible conflict situation. Now my question to you is: Although you say the civilian police had authority to detain HV, in practice it was different on the ground. Now, is this the reason why the civilian police could not apprehend members of the HV committing crimes in the absence of military police because if the civilian police tried to do that, members of the HV would threaten them with arms and there could be a possible conflict? Is that what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I never said that the police had the authority to detain HV members. It could only retain them until further notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, even if this is correct, you certainly have understood what the core of the question was. Whether your testimony of yesterday, that it depended on the assessment of the civilian police officers, whether or not they would take the risk of a conflict with HV members when intervening, whether that is to be understood as a similar or the same thing as what you said during this meeting, that during the second stage that - and let me literally, because it disappeared from my screen - that "parts of units burnt houses and threatened with arms, if tried to be prevented from committing crimes." That sounds rather similar as not accepting an intervention at check-points, a risk of a conflict. Now, are you talking about the same kind of things here at this meeting as you told us yesterday about what would happen at check-points?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember the conversation going that way. But it was only reasonable that if there was threat at a certain check-point or danger of a quarrel, or a clash, that, in such a case, the police would choose not to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that were the kind of events you talked about during this is meeting as well. Is that ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If could I just state one thing, but if I could ask if the witness understands English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Cetina, do you understand the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please take your earphones off for a second. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wouldn't normally do this, but in light of the fact that I anticipate we're going have an issue of -- of time and we're going to try to complete this witness's testimony today, I did want to state that if there's going to be an issue of whether the police could act against HV members in this line of questioning, then I will ask for some time in re-cross because I believe this issue has been covered extensively through the trial with examples. So I don't know if that's the case, but I did want to let the Prosecution know that I will ask for time to put that to him if it's going to be an issue as to whether the civilian police not only had the authority to do it but actually was doing it at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We've heard the evidence the witness gave yesterday in respect of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wasn't intending to explore deeply into this subject, I just wanted to do exactly what I just did just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then please proceed. We'll ask the witness to put his earphones on again. Mr. Cetina, could you ... Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, just one last question on that, Mr. Cetina. Now, at this meeting you -- I'm sorry just going back. Yesterday, repeatedly, you responded to Mr. Misetic that, in practice, the civilian police did not or could not apprehend or address crimes by military --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. Let me just withdraw that. I don't want to get into a long debate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, now, according to these minutes, you have articulated this problem at this meeting. You have, in fact, said exactly that -- that this problem was that -- that members of the HV were committing crimes and threatened with arms if they were -- if there was an attempt to prevent them. Now, at this meeting, there were members of the military police present, particularly the commander, Colonel Budimir, and we will go through what he said in the next page. Now, how did the military police respond to that statement you made? Was there any further discussion on that matter?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall any further discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did the police force attempt to address this issue with any members or any commanders of the HV, the fact that, when the police attempted to prevent crime, the -- the units that were staying in the area tried to respond with arms?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object again. That's not -- that's a mischaracterisation of what is written in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me rephrase, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you please perhaps use the exact language as we find it in the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now you have reported that, in the second stage, that the stay of parts of the units which burnt houses and thereafter -- therefore with arms if tried to prevent from committing crimes. There are -- I'm sorry, and threatened with arms if tried to prevent -- if tried to be prevented from committing crimes. Now this issue, where the units were burning houses --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Objection again, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm not saying anything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first allow Ms. Mahindaratne to carefully think about the phrasing of her question and to finish her question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, was that issue placed before any commanders of the HV?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Same objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The issue was -- the issue as we find it in the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is apparently what Ms. Mahindaratne is talking about. And the question is whether this issue was placed before HV and that's -- I do not see what's wrong with that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm just objecting -- to me, there is a distinction between units --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. The issue -- the issue as we find in the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's how I rephrase it --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was the issue as we find it in these minutes, where it says that - and I'll -- the issue being that "parts of units that had stayed which burnt houses and threatened with arms if tried to be prevented from committing crimes." Was that issue raised with HV commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't in touch with the commanders, and I, myself, did not raise that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware of anyone else raising it with HV commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, beyond raising this matter at this meeting in Plitvice on 15th of September, what did you, as the head of the police administration of Zadar-Knin, do to address that problem?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We informed our heads at the ministry who were present there and tried to do our job as best we could, on our own.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, that problem that you reported here at this meeting, what was the basis for your information? Was that based on reports you have received from your subordinate officers, the police commanders?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an impression made on the basis of the reports we received and forwarded to the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, were you informed as to how the civilian police on the ground reacted in those particular situations, when they were threatened with arms, when they tried to prevent crimes, by members of the HV?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that the police, in the cases where they assessed that a conflict might occur, refrained from reacting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, moving on, Mr. Cetina. Yesterday your testimony, or the day before, during direct examination, your testimony was that you were aware that there was a shortage of military police for patrols within the Kotar-Knin Police Administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is at transcript page T23421 going to 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In fact you had reported that at this meeting too.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if you could move to the next page, page 4.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask Ms. Mahindaratne to speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My apologies. If we could move to page 4, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There we also have Colonel Budimir also speaking at this meeting, and he reports -- said Colonel Mihael Budimir, commander of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, Split: "Call attention to the spatially large area of responsibility covered by the 72nd Military Police Battalion and did not agree with opinions that there was not enough manpower. The co-operation with the MUP was disturbed but only in some individual cases. State of security, public order, and road traffic safety reached the satisfying level, and with returns of civilian population in Knin, a problem with disposal of rubbish occurred?" Now, Mr. Budimir obviously does not agree with your opinion that there was a shortage of manpower, of military personnel. Would you -- wouldn't you agree with me that the commander of the 72nd Military Police Battalion would know more about the manning levels within his battalion than yourself?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment on what her [as interpreted] perception of the matter was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm not asking to you comment, Mr. Cetina, my question is: Wouldn't you agree with me that the commander of the military police battalion would know more about his own manning levels than yourself?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, in fact, on this subject, when Mr. Kay questioned you --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this is transcript page 23.429.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "But this problem here, within the Kotar-Knin Police Administration concerning the number of military police, was that something that you were aware of at the time?" And your responses is: "Yes, in a way, yes. Well, that means if an agreement had been reached at a higher level, then, on the ground, they either acted as best they could or had a shortage of men." So is it correct, then, based on that answer -- would you agree with me that your opinion on the manning levels of the military police was based on the fact that there was no cooperation forthcoming from the military police? Was that the basis on which you concluded that they were short-staffed?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't have a sufficient manning level. My assessment was that, in view of the number of check-points, they weren't able to provide us with sufficient numbers of men to man the check-points.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did Colonel Budimir ever inform you of that fact? Did he ever tell you, I can't send you these people because I don't have sufficient men?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. We set up check-points together. For instance, we set up 15 check-points, and they sent their men only to three of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So it is on that basis that you concluded that they were short-staffed, because they didn't send men to all 15?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do wonder about this line of cross-examinations. We looked at a number of documents yesterday where it wasn't Mr. Budimir who was giving an explanation. It was Mr. Primorac, the deputy, there were other military police officers at meetings. Not only with the Zadar-Knin Police Administration but Kotar-Knin Police Administrations, whose records were recorded. And I think the proper way of dealing with this, rather than putting Mr. Budimir's name to the witness, would be if the Prosecution referred to those recorded documents and statements by the military police officers to the police. Otherwise, a totally misleading impression is given of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, apparently, has chosen a very limited approach to this matter and, of course, the Chamber will understand all the evidence in the context of which it was put to a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. In those circumstances, then, Your Honour, I understand the position.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm merely testing this -- the knowledge of this witness, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just told you that you apparently have chosen a certain approach, and the Chamber will, of course, evaluate the whole of the evidence. And if this portion of the evidence is linked only -- not to all of the remainder, then the evidence should be understood in the context in which it was elicited by you from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, moving on, let me take to you your statement given to the OTP, and that's D1745. In page 9, paragraph 4, this is what you say. Perhaps if you want to follow your statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if you could just -- D1745.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is what you say: "The uniformed police were not often visiting the villages situated at a distance from the main roads. That is why the main sources of information about the crimes committed in the villages were members of the civilian protection and representatives of the international organisations." And then ...

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you see that? In page ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, D1745.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm reading your statement given to the OTP, Mr. Cetina.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: B/C/S page number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I have a minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: About page -- this is not the -- in the English, if you could get to page 9. Let me just ... not this page. If I could have assistance from ... Mr. Registrar, if you could move to the next page, I think that might be ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, what about in the B/C/S version, page 7, the semi-last paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I ... Yes, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that be a suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, I think we need page 9 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In -- even in B/C/S, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want to refer to the paragraph which starts with "meetings with representatives," then I strongly suggest that you look at page 7 in the B/C/S version, semi-last paragraph, starting at "Sastanak s predstavnicima ..." Don't ask me to further pronounce it. That seems to be the paragraph you were referring to in English on page 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's already on the screen, so we don't have to wait much longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yeah, it's already on the screen. Thank you, Mr. President. My apologies for not having the B/C/S page number.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you see that, Mr. Cetina? And then, if we could go to the next page, page 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first verify. Mr. Cetina, have you read that paragraph and have you followed the portion quoted by Ms. Mahindaratne? "Sources of information ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes? Then let's now move to the next page then. And please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Next page, Mr. Cetina, if you focus on that paragraph that starts with "In respect of the UNCIVPOL ..." that is in the Croatian version page 3 -- paragraph 3. There are -- the last four sentence it is says -- last four lines: "Everything reported to us by the international organisations was good for us, because we could investigates all that. The information from the monitors helped us because most of the murders were in remote hamlets, not on the main roads. The police were not going off the main roads very much at that time." That's your testimony. Now, as I understand your evidence, the international organisations were bringing in these reports to the police because they were patrolling these areas -- those areas. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So, now, if the international organisations and the civilian protection could patrol those areas, what was the problem for the civilian police to patrol those areas, particularly giving -- considering your own testimony that most of the murders were being committed in the -- those areas?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already said, there weren't enough personnel to cover that vast an area. The perception expressed here is that we used all sort of information that we came by from international organisations and civilian protection. Let me tell you that we did not rely only upon police information in all these cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, your testimony is also that, when you went to Kistanje, that Kistanje was already destroyed. That is in the OTP statement, for the record, page 14, the first paragraph. And you said when you left -- went to Kistanje, that most features were burnt before you got there. Now, my question is: When did you go to Kistanje for the first time?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the first several days I went through Kistanje, in fact, in perhaps the ten days.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you be more specific. When you say the first few days, "first several days," what was the -- when was the first day you entered Kistanje? Was it the 5th, the 6th?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on the 5th or the 6th.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: 7th?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because in those days, I would come via Drnis, though I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said that "the first several days I went through Kistanje." Could you give the Trial Chamber some idea as to around when. Is it after one week after the completion of the operation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that the completion of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has already answered that he is not certain about whether it was not on the 7th already.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was the last part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, your testimony is that Kistanje was destroyed, you say, during Storm. What did you mean by that? "During Storm." What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I meant was that it didn't happen in a day. It happened over a period of time, a month or two. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. But you said, Mr. Cetina, that when you visited Kistanje for the first time it was already destroyed. So are you then able to give us some idea as to, you know, whether you went to Kistanje after one month, after two months, because I'm trying to give the Trial Chamber some idea as to when you saw Kistanje as being completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the month and a half that I was there, I passed through Kistanje on three or four occasions, and I can say that it happened over a period of time, not all at once.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So what did you do about Kistanje? What type of investigations did you carry out to find out what the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, wouldn't we first -- shouldn't we first try to find out exactly what the statement says. I read to you what your statement says: "In respect of Kistanje, as far as I know, it was destroyed during Storm. When I first went there, it was already destroyed." Now, you just told us that you're not certain whether it was in these early day, whether it was already on the 7th - that is a possibility, apparently. Now to say, Kistanje was destroyed a period of two months, that seems to contradict what we find in your statement, where you say "when I first went there, it was already destroyed," and you consider it possible that that was already on the 7th, passing through. And that's the language you used. So could you please clarify this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may. If I could just call your attention to page 21, paragraph 3 -- line 3, I should say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the last being: "Though I don't remember."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If he could be asked to clarify that because I think he -- as I understand it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, let's -- You were asked about the 7th, you -- whether you had been in Kistanje already. And then you said: "No. Because in those days, I would come via Drnis." Though you do not remember. What did you not remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember passing through Kistanje -- or, rather, I definitely did not go through Kistanje the first time I travelled to Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But on the 7th, would you consider it possible that you went through Kistanje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Because I did not go to Knin two times in a row.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And, now, what did you not remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember -- or, rather, I believe that in the first ten days I did go to Kistanje once. But when was it? Definitely not in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, let's just -- let's take this as a starting point. If you went to Kistanje within the first ten days, although not in the very first ones but perhaps the 11th or the 12th, and you say the first time you came there, you went there, it was already destroyed. And now you tell us that the destruction took place over a period of two month; whereas, your statement clearly suggests that the destruction was already there when you came there for the first time, which, as you just told us, would have been anywhere between the 7th, 8th, or the 13th, 14th of August. Could you explain this, what seems, at first sight, to be a contradiction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't count the houses that were burned or destroyed. However, I can certainly say, from my memory, that the majority was destroyed in the first 10 to 15 days. Then later on, I never stopped in Kistanje. I merely passed through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you're telling us is that most part of the destruction in Kistanje took place not over a period of two month, but within the first ten days, or perhaps ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I would say that that's the closest to the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if there's any way to come closer, please tell us. Ms. Mahindaratne, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Kistanje, Mr. Cetina, is within your area of responsibility. Now, upon observing this destruction, what did you, as head of the police administration, do to investigate as to what the causes of the destruction were and who had committed that crime?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that there were no eye-witnesses, it was very difficult to uncover the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So was any investigation carried out at all? Any on-site investigations at all?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every piece of information that was helpful was checked. The better part of the information can be found at the police administration in the relevant documentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did you instruct your subordinate officers to call from the military any information as to what units were deployed in Kistanje during the period when it was possibly destroyed?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had never had information to the effect that it was the army that perpetrated the deed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, now you're telling the Trial Chamber that most of the features in Kistanje were destroyed when you went. And you know that a military operation had been conducted in the area. Now, don't you think, as a police officer, one of the first steps either to find the potential perpetrators or potential witnesses, what you should have done was to find out if there were any members of the military present in the vicinity of the crime site? Wouldn't that be a logical step to take in the course of an investigation?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If something was damaged in a war operation, then it becomes a different matter. The police acts where crimes have been committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in your mind, when you saw the destruction in Kistanje, what did you conclude? That it happened in a war operation or that it was a crime?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not an expert in war operations, but I could see that the houses were set on fire and destroyed. As for any other perception… I cannot give you that. Nor the way it was done or by whom - I don’t know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So were you -- what steps did you take - I'm asking you to tell the Trial Chamber what steps did you take to find out as to who set these houses on fire with Zoljas? What kind of investigative steps did you take?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, there were set on fire by what?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It has been written as "fire by Zoljas," and maybe I didn't pronounce -- Z-o-l-j-a-s. That's your answer. Your answer was: "I am not an expert in war operations, but I could see that the houses were set on fire by Zoljas." And I believe that is a sort of weapon.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Croatian translation, I don't see where it says Zoljas. Could you please indicate that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, your answer was translated that you could see that - not in your statement but what you just told us - that could you see that the houses were set on fire by Zoljas. That's how your answer to one of the previous questions was translated to us. And you said: "That's all can I tell you." Mr. Kay, I'm referring to page 25, lines 19 and following.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have information that the word "soldiers" was not used -- "Zoljas," sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which -- Mr. Cetina, you answered: "I am not an expert in war operations, but I could see that the houses were set on fire by ..." And what did you then say? You don't have to look at your screen. If you just tell us what you -- one of the answers was. And I quoted 95 per cent of your answer, and I asked you to repeat the word you then used.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw that they were damaged and set on fire. I don't know what else to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you said something earlier. You said: "I am not an expert ... but the only thing I can tell you is that they were set on fire by ..." By what? By whom, by what? By -- what did you then say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say by what means it was done. I went through the town and that is what I could see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you remember that answer, which you -- the answer starting with --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, my -- I was actually having to deal with something else at the time. But I'm advised that nothing was said. And maybe this should be an instance where the tape is looked at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps we should do that. I'll ask it once again to clarify the issue -- to see whether we can see -- clarify the issue without playing the audio or checking the audio. Let me just find it again. I repeat question and the answer, although not complete, as it was given to us in translation and in our transcript. The question that was put to you by Ms. Mahindaratne reads on our transcript as follows: "Now, in your mind, when you saw the destruction in Kistanje, what did you conclude? That it happened in a war operation or that it was a crime?" And your answer, as we find it on our screens, is as follows: "I am not an expert in war operations, but I could see that the houses were set on fire by ..." And then you used the word. And then you continued by saying: "That is all I can tell you. I can't tell you anything about who may have done it or anything else for that matter." We do understand what you cannot tell us, but what was the one thing that you said you could see? That the houses were set on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably "destroyed." I may have said that word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think we'll have to check the audio to find out what exactly the answer was. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cetina, in your statement given to the OTP, the Office of the Prosecutor, you also go on to say that -- say this: "I did unfortunately see burning houses."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is the last page, for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "We were in the field to familiarise ourselves with the situation. We did our very best to stop the looting and burning." Now, my question is: When you saw burning houses in the course of your visits in the field, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, we always saw such houses from a distance. I seldom passed by a house that was on flames at that very moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, do I understand your answer to be that you -- the houses you saw burning were from a distance and that you didn't pass by those houses? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, I did not pass by a house at the moment, as it burned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So did you see them in a distance -- in the distance? Is that what you're saying? You saw the burning houses --

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So then you -- why were you were going near those houses? Because they were burning or why?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I went to meetings. I was on my way there, and I informed those subordinated to me that they should check on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And then, thereafter, did you follow up and ask your subordinates as to what -- whether they have checked, what they found, whether any investigation has been initiated?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, given the staffing strength, they were supposed to check what the situation was about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you clarify that? When you say, "in any case, given the staffing strength," that's not my question to you. Whether you followed up your information to your subordinates -- did you call up your subordinate officers and ask them what they had done, what investigative steps they had taken, or you just left it at that. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, I was supposed to be informed in the -- by their summary reports. I did not have time to discuss each and every event with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So I take your answer to be, no, that you did not follow up by ask -- by questioning them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not. They did report to me. But there were many events, and I definitely was not acquainted with each and every one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you give us a specific example of an instance where you saw a burning house and you ordered one of your subordinate officers to go and investigate? I'm not asking you for date, time, but perhaps the name of a subordinate officer you asked to investigate and the location of the burning house?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't give you that. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, when you informed your subordinate officers, would that information be recorded in the -- the log-books of the police stations? You know, saying, Chief Cetina has informed that a house was burning at such and such a location. You know how it is recorded in the police log-books.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what they put into the log-books. I did not check such matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Moving on, Mr. Cetina. Now, yesterday you were shown an order issued by the Assistant Minister, Mr. Moric.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if I could have D49 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And there was some discussion about a specific order contained in that document. Sorry, it wasn't yesterday; day before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if you could go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, looking at this order, you were, yesterday, questioned by the Presiding Judge on this particular order, with regard to point 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If could you, on the Croatian version, Mr. Registrar, go to page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this is at transcript page 23415. Now, with regard to this order you were asked: "My question was whether you then considered this order to be in violation of the existing legislation." Your response was: "In a certain way, it is not, in fact, in accordance with the law." Again you were asked a question: "So, in a certain way, it's a violation of the law." You responded: "In a way, yes." Now -- you're shaking your head, Mr. Cetina. Are you agreeing with me or disagreeing with something I said? I just merely read out to you an exchange between yourself and the Presiding Judge the day before yesterday. I haven't asked you a question yet.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer to the Judge's question was that, Yes, in a way it was a violation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct. That's what I was going ask you now. What you testified here is that the assistant minister has issued you and the other chiefs of the police administration an illegal order, a law in -- an order in contravention of the law. Now, this -- did you discuss that fact with the other officers of the Ministry of Interior, either with Mr. Moric himself or any other assistant ministers, or the minister, Mr. Jarnjak, the fact that you have received an illegal order, which you in fact testified that you ignored? Did you discuss that matter?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall discussing it with anyone. But I was not bound by that item. The Law on the Interior states that once I receive an official order, which would be illegal, I am under no obligation to implement it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That you have -- you categorically stated here. But my question is: Was there any formal conversation at least between yourself and the other colleagues, the other chiefs of police administration, as to how you should respond or what to do about when you received an illegal order from an assistant minister?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, the previous answer started: "I don't recall discussing it with anyone." That is an answer to your question. Of course, if there is any reason why you would want to put that question again, then can you can do so. But any reason --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I note that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then -- yes, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I withdraw that question, Mr. President. I don't need this document any further, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cetina, I'm moving on to another area. Yesterday, Mr. Mikulicic questioned you about the special police. And you, in fact, have given a comprehensive statement about your authority over the special police. And this is in your statement to the OTP. This is what you say: "There were also so-called special police units. They were not under the command of the police administration but were directly answerable to the MUP."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: For the record, this is D1745, page 4, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "They had a different building, different uniforms, and they were not doing regular police duties. According to the law, in peacetime, the professional tasks were the prevention of bigger unrest resolving, hijacking, kidnapping, and similar jobs. When I arrived in Zadar to take up my post, such a unit already existed there. I did not know what their tasks were, if they had any, which they coordinated directly with the MUP headquarters. I personally was not involved in drafting their plans. "The special police units had also existed in the former Yugoslavia. I believe their tasks were related to anti-terrorism and hostage situations. The commander of the special police units in Zadar was Svemir Vrsaljko." Pardon my pronunciation. "I do not know how many people were under his command. I have never been informed about the special tasks undertaken by those special police units. I never had any meetings with representatives of the special police units. At the time of Storm, I had no control over the special police. The police system that I was in was designed for peacetime, not wartime." Is that correct, that you had no control over the special police unit -- units?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a way, yes. They were professionally under the ministry, but were also a part of the Knin and Zadar Police Administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, after the completion of the initial attack in Operation Storm - and that would be 6th or 7th August - there were mop-up operations carried out to clear the terrain by the special police forces. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, as the head of the police administration, did you have any role to play in those mop-up operation, either planning or deciding where those operations were being carried out or issuing orders to the special police units to carry out some of those mop-up operations?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in terms of planning and organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What was the role that you played in those mop-up operations?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I may have been informed that there was an ensuing activity in a certain area, but I wasn't familiar with anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, were you involved in issuing any orders to the special police recording those mop-up operations?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were you involved in issuing any orders to the special police units attached to your police administration which were deployed in the initial attack during the operation itself?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, would it be correct to say that the instances when you had authority over special police units attached to your police administration was when they were utilized to assist the regular police in carrying out the regular police work which were more peacetime duties.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In peacetime, in any case, they were used to resolve complex situations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, my question is: Your authority, if at all, was used -- I'm sorry, I withdraw that question. Now, when you mentioned the word "complex situations," can you clarify what you were talking about it? Was it only during peacetime, or were you involved in utilizing the special police for any wartime activity?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had such complex situations in mind which would entail a degree of drain for which regular police were not trained.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: For example, a hostage-taking situation or the stake-out that was discussed yesterday? That type of situation?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Hostage situations, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you were questioned about your disciplinary authority over employees of your police force. Did you have disciplinary authority over members of the special police forces?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, referring to your disciplinary authority - this is at page 16 of yesterday's proceedings - Mr. Mikulicic asked you what type of disciplinary authority you had over your special police forces and you said -- this is what you said. I will quote you. You said: "My only power" -- this is at page 26, my apologies. "My only power was to file a request for the initiation of a disciplinary procedure." This is what you said with regard to your disciplinary authority over your police forces. Now, isn't it correct that if a member of the special police forces committed an offence, that request for disciplinary procedures, initiation of disciplinary procedures, had to be made by the commander of the special police sector and not yourself?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I have, Mr. Registrar, document D1762, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, this is a document that was shown to you by Mr. Mikulicic yesterday. And it's from the assistant minister going to the police administrations. And it says: "In case of an enemy attack on supervisory control points on patrols as well as all intelligence security information, events or occurrences, you are obliged to urgently inform the special police sector on the special telephone." And the numbers are given. The reference there to the special police sector is to the special police sector command, isn't it? You're supposed to contact either Mr. Markac or Mr. Sacic. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. This would be a good time for a break, and I have very little time to take afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will have a break, and we will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, in your statement given to the Defence --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this is, for the record, D1743, in paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- you have addressed sanitation work and the burial procedures involved. And this is what you say. This is at page 8 of the statement. You said: "The team for the clearing up of the terrain assessed objectively whether the cause of death was murder or war operations. There were cases when it was reported to the police that a body had been found." Now, first, a clarification, when you say "they assessed objectively whether the cause of death was murder or war operations," by the term "war operations," you mean whether a person had died in the course of combat duty due to being caught up in a cross-fire or that type of activity, as opposed to an execution. Isn't that correct? That's what you mean by "war operations"?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general meaning of war operations. I can't really go into the details, whether it was the cross-fire or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. So what you mean is that a person had been killed in the course of combat as opposed to an execution. Isn't that what you meant by that term?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, can you -- can you clarify to the Trial Chamber as to how exactly that determination was made. What was the criteria that was applied by the clearing-up teams in determining if a person had died in the course of combat or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of Interior issued instructions to the civilian protection service or, rather, to the teams engaged in sanitisation about the procedure they should follow. I was not that involved in the issue and was not familiar with their modus operandi. They were within the hierarchy of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, wouldn't you agree with me that to arrive at that determination as to what -- whether a person had died in the course of combat or whether it's an a murder, it would necessarily require an on-site investigation at the location where the body was recovered?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: An on-site investigation is part of an investigation, that's right. And if the case involved war operations, then there was no need for on-site investigations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. But even -- even to determine if a person had died in the course of combat, wouldn't you require an on-site investigation? Otherwise, how would one determine as to what circumstances had led to the death?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was done by the teams out in the field, and they made the relevant assessments. I was not involved in specific cases, so I can't tell you more than I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge, were on-site investigations conducted into every body that was discovered in the aftermath of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On-site investigations within the meaning of the Law on Criminal Procedure, no, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And who directed that on-site investigations need not be carried out?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zidovec drafted instruction as to the manner of the conduct of the sanitisation of human bodies. He was assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in your statement to the Defence you said this - and this is in paragraph 16. You say: "The team for clearing up as a rule would include an officer of the crime police, one officer each from all the services that are able to make decisions, and a forensic pathologist." Now what was the role of the officer from the crime police within the sanitation teams? What was his role?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were part of the team, and they were under strict instructions from the ministry. I cannot go into the details of it, since I'm not familiar with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, the crime police in the Zadar-Knin Police Administration comes under your jurisdiction - isn't it? - they're your subordinate officers. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, your subordinate officers are sent out to the field as part of a team, and is it your position that you didn't know what they were doing out there? You didn't know why -- as to why your subordinate officers were made a part of a team?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of the Interior. And it was in this way that the teams were formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you had no information at all from your crime police officers as to what they were doing within the sanitation teams. That's your evidence?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew the number of the individuals processed in the field, but I did not discuss the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, were you aware that a decision had been taken, in fact, by the crime police not to carry out on-site investigations in the course of the sanitation work?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And I refer to, for the record, evidence D234, D235, and D236, for the information of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you aware that there was a decision not to carry out on-site investigations prior to the disposal of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me show you a document, Mr. Cetina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I have D235, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you notice, Mr. Cetina, that in paragraph 1 it says: "Since, in the area of the army activity, war operations are being conducted, it is crucial to carry out clearing up the terrain in that area and it is our task to carry out the identification of persons in the prescribed manner. And it is not necessary to conduct on-site investigations. Mr. Maric will carry out coordination of the above." Now, you didn't know about this?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not aware of the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I have P2652, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were not involved in any substantial way in the sanitation work. But were you -- were you involved in exhuming bodies that been disposed of in an incorrect manner?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you explain -- do you recognise the document that is on your screen?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that it bears my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You say you can see that it bears your signature, meaning you don't recollect the document -- have you no recollection of this document, or do you admit that it's a document written by you? What are you exactly saying when you say that it bears your signature?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document which does not have an actual signature of mine is a coded message, and it contains a letter written by someone, I suppose it was Mr. Batur, who signed documents on the sanitisation of human bodies on my behalf.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that Mr. Batur signed documents and you were not aware of the subject matter of this letter that he signed on your behalf? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could so happen that if I was not present in the police administration, and very often I was not, and he had to send a report to the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cetina, are you familiar at all with the content of this document, the subject matter of this document? Do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Moving on, Mr. Cetina. Were you involved in monitoring the collection centres in your area of responsibility, where civilians and/or prisoners of war were kept?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can I have P904, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: As you will see in a moment, Mr. Cetina, a document written by you, relating to collection centres. And you can already see the Croatian version on your screen. It's sent to Operation Povratak to the Ministry of the Interior headquarters and your sending it in response in relation to a document, telegram dated 4th August, 1994. You -- this is what you report: "Up to 0500 hours on 6 August 1995, the following prisoners are in the collection centre."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And then, Mr. Registrar, if we could move to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Then have you a list of persons and the you say: "There are 135 elderly people and children in the holding centre." And there is further explanation, and you have signed this document. Now, we examined this document, Mr. Cetina. First of all, let me ask you this: Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am. But I didn't sign it. And I can see it now, that I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you -- was it somebody who had signed this document on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody signed and was authorised to do so, but I can't recognise the signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cetina, if someone signs a document on your behalf, do you consider it as a document issued by you, or are you claiming -- are you washing your hands of that document?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't wash my hands of it. I trusted my associates.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Then -- I can tell you that we've gone through this document and amongst that first category of people where you say the following prisoners are in the collection centre, there is a list of persons. There are a number of elderly people recorded as prisoners there. For example, number 4, we're going by the dates of birth, number 6, number 7, 8, 12, et cetera. Now, can you explain to the Trial Chamber why elderly people were being held as prisoners in these collection centres?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that they were members of units or were known as perpetrators of criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, there is, at page -- number 8, for example, a person born in 1922 being held as a prisoner. Is it your position that these elderly people were also considered as being members of units of the RSK? That your position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, does it make any sense that where the witness said it was either for this reason or another reason then to go first through the one which seems to be less obvious? Why not ask the witness in what of the two categories this person was, if he knows.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You heard the question. Of the two categories that you mentioned, that they were either members of units or were known to be perpetrators of criminal offences, are you able to, for example, say the person, for example, registered at number 8, who was born in 1922, in what capacity he was being held?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, the ages may not necessarily be significant when it comes to these considerations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, could you please answer the question. Do you know the reason why this person born in 1922 was detained as a prisoner? Do you know? If so, please tell us; if you don't know, please, tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told you what my opinion was, and my answer to this question is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Then on the second page --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if you could go to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- you also record that there are 135 elderly people and children in the holding centre. Now, why were elderly people and children being kept in a holding centre? And I'm using the term that you have used. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Word "kept" does not appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd also --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Why would they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's apparently what you would like to ask the witness. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd also ask that we check the translation of the word "holding," because I think it is important to what the original actually says, and it's a term that the Chamber will be familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could I invite -- I know that this is not the way to verify translations. At the same time, if we ask for a formal review of the translation, then the witness might have been gone. So let's, as a preliminary and exceptional exercise, could I invite a native-speaking person -- or could I ask the witness -- Could you please slowly read the first sentence which comes after item 23 which apparently start with "u prihvatnom Centru ..." Could you read that line -- that sentence slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In the reception centre, there are 135 elderly persons and children."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, moving on to another area. In your testimony given to the OTP, you have addressed the case of Varivode and Gosici, you know, as one of the crimes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, if -- sorry for interrupting you. Does this mean that you're not interested to hear from this witness why 135 elderly people and children were in a reception centre?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Going back to the issue we were discussing, the Varivode and Gosici case, you have referred to as one of the crimes solved by one of your officers. And, in fact, you have said that it was initiated by you and you're very proud of the outcome. Isn't it correct that the principle basis on which the accused were charged in relation to both those cases, Varivode and Gosici murders, were their own confessions made to the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what reached the investigating judge. We are not a party appearing before the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, this Trial Chamber has heard a lot of evidence of the Varivode and Gosici case, and, in fact, those judgements are also in evidence. Now, are you -- now have you, in fact, taken credit for that case as being one of the cases that you initiated and your officers solved. Now, are you then aware that the basis on which they were charged was the confessions made by the accused to the investigative judge? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. In the preliminary proceedings, they did make a confession, but I don't recall what happened from there on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, are you aware that the trial court acquitted the accused in relation to that case? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, in the statement given to the OTP, you, in fact, claim credit for these two cases. And you're still -- now telling the Trial Chamber that you don't even know the outcome of these cases. Is that what you are saying? The basis on which the persons were charged.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with what happened until the end of the preliminary proceedings. Thereupon, I left Zadar and I didn't know what -- which course the proceedings took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, I'm wondering what the relevance is of knowing whether this witness rightly or wrongly claims any credit for the work done in relation to this case. Is that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
