utterances.text: No, Mr. President, it's was just that there is evidence to the effect, before the Trial Chamber, that, in fact, that case has not -- was not, in fact, solved. I'm just addressing Court to testimony of Witness Zganjer. I don't know whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, the only thing I'm asking, what is the relevance of whether this witness is right or wrong in claiming or at least saying that his service did a good job - whether it was a good job or bad job, we can consider that - but what's the relevance?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's the credibility of this witness, Mr. President, that I was testing. But I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, I have only a couple more questions to you. And I --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If we could have, Mr. Registrar, D1745.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's the statement that you made to the Office of the Prosecutor. And this is in the English page 11, paragraph 4; and in the Croatian version, page 9, paragraph 4. Now, this is -- you talk about police -- authority of the police officers in addressing crimes. "The police were not allowed by law to search someone or their vehicle without a court order. You could stop and check someone in civilian clothes, but you could not search that person. If, for example, the police pulled over a car and found a weapon in the trunk, and if they did not have a court order, then the evidence would be dismissed for any subsequent court proceedings." And I'm trying to understand your testimony, Mr. Cetina. Now, according to what you say, if a person in a vehicle, be it a civilian or a soldier, was stopped at a civilian police check-point, and if that civilian police officer could see that the vehicle was carrying goods, such as TVs and radios, suspected looted goods, are you saying that he cannot search the vehicle and take that into custody without a court order, or is that not what you meant -- meant to say in the statement?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to answer it. If the object of a crime is visible, then this could be deemed as a checking procedure and would be valid before a court of law. However, if the evidence of a crime needs prior searching of the vehicle or the premises, then this is something that requires a court order.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So, as such, according to what you say, the police had the -- there was no impediment for the police to take into custody looted goods, if detected, at a civilian check-point. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, on -- I need -- just seeking further clarification -- a similar one --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is the same statement, page 14, paragraph 2 in the English version, and in the Croatian version, page 11, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You said that: "You ask about crimes and how they were recorded when complaints were made to the MUP by civilians. And if crimes were reported that were committed by soldiers, then the person who reported the crime would have been told that if soldiers were involved, it had to be reported to the military police. Those were the applicable rules. I concede that ... MUP could have recorded the reports. I'm not denying. But they did nothing wrong in saying that the matter be reported to the military police." So was it the case when a civilian goes to the nearest police station or to the nearest civilian policemen and reports that military -- a member of the army or somebody in military uniform was seen in committing a crime, they would be asked to go and report the matter to the military police. Is that what you're saying here?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, this is what we did. We would inform the military police if there were indications that HV members may be suspected of having committed a crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. I probably -- you're properly misunderstood here. So what you're saying here is that you, the police, would then inform the military police, not ask the complainant to go to the military police?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne. Mr. Kay, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But before we do so, I would like to inform the parties that at the request of the Chamber the famous "Zolja" line has been reviewed and as a result - and this will be later confirmed in an official memo - but as matters stand now, what the witness said - and this is also for you, Mr. Cetina, because there was quite a bit of confusion about those lines. As matters stand now, the Chamber understands that you said the following: "I am not an expert in war operations, but I could see that the houses were set on fire and destroyed. As for any other perception, I cannot give you that, nor the way it was done or by whom, I don't know." Now, I was also informed that it took a while -- it needed listening a couple of times before -- in reviewing this text, those who did this job were able to exactly hear and that there apparently was a word which, at least, has a Z and an O in it as well, which may have caused the confusion. But I think now it's clear that all the questions about Zoljas or soldiers, or whatever, are moot. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I can claim no credit, as I was on the wrong track totally at the time, and others informed me of the matter, Your Honour. So I thank you them for their keen ears on the matter. Re-examination now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at a document, please, Mr. Cetina. It's D1756.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, could you kindly get closer to the microphone, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a letter that was sent from the International Committee of the Red Cross to General Cermak, and you can see your name is -- is written on the top in handwriting. And the word "urgent." "Mr. Cetina, urgent." And if we go -- if we could just look at the content of this page, the author is asking personal intervention: "We expect results of the investigation following our verbal and written reports. We" -- and is reminding again about serious incidents reported to our personnel during visits to neighbouring villages. So this is the Red Cross, writing to General Cermak and expecting results of investigation following our verbal and written reports. And then we see, on the next page, a list of places: Golubic, the 6th of September; Ridjane; Ridjane; Varivode, with details from the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Further details. And at E, Zrmanja. Again, all of which are reports of crimes. And then on the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can turn to the last page. We seem to have a problem on the screen, Your Honour. I do. Does anyone else? There we are. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you can see here in the last sentence: "Thank you for your personal intervention, and in expectation of results, send you our regards." This letter, then, which has your name on it, came to General Cermak and is a list of serious crimes that had occurred which the Red Cross expected to have information about and results. Do you recollect receiving this document with these particular incidents as identified?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I am unable to see the last page you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There's the -- oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If it could be blown up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you read that now?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't see the page at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There was something on our screens that indicated some sort of problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is the last page, signed by someone called Carmen Burger. And as I pointed out, has the: "Thank you for your personal intervention, and in expectation of results ..." Can you see that? You can't see anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If can I have a hard copy while others ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If can you still get it out, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness sees it, he says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you able to see it now? Can you see the name Carmen Burger?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would you like to go back to the beginning of the document? Would that help you? We've had an interruption here.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could go back to the first page. It's Exhibit D1756. In Croatian, if anyone has got a Croatian language version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you see that on the screen now, the big screen?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Cetina, urgent, 7th of September, 1995. Letter to General Cermak. And this letter "expects results of the investigation following our verbal and written reports." Do you recollect receiving this letter forwarded to you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And we've looked at what was inside the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we turn now to P2649.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you see that, Mr. Cetina? This is a letter dated the 10th of October. It actually comes from you. And it's for the attention of General Cermak. And it's in reply to the request of the International Red Cross Organisation for submission of data on incidents. "We hereby advise you we've completed the necessary checks regarding each event mentioned in the letter." And we see there the places set out: Golubic; Ridjane; Ridjane; Varivode.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Zrmanja. And your response to each of those particular incidents -- for instance, if we look at Zrmanja, a thorough criminal investigation is being conducted into all the murders and with the object of identifying the unknown perpetrators. So looking at this chain of events, was Mr. Cermak ordering you to investigate; or was he doing something else, in relation to the information provided to him by the Red Cross? Perhaps you can describe it.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not see it as an order. He simply requested notification, given that the original request was put in by the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was Mr. Cermak doing anything wrong by forwarding this information to you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was he putting himself in a position whereby he was commanding you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we just go and look, then, at one of the incidents. If we can -- which was referred to as being the Simo Dokic matter. If we go to 65 ter 2D00770.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This predates the response to Mr. Cermak, but it's from the crime police department to the 72nd Police Department, dated 18th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I hate to interrupt, by I wonder whether we could have the English document also on the screen. I hope I'm not creating any trouble for the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have some trouble in showing all the documents on the screen, and that's why, as Mr. Registrar informed me, we have found a kind of a solution which, first of all, serves the witness to have access. Ms. Mahindaratne, I take it that this is a released document in e-court by the Defence which you can consult.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will follow -- I will follow through my own personal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And, of course, the Chamber is a bit handicapped here as well but ... Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will just repeat the number if it helps people, 65 ter 2D00770.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm just giving people a bit of time, Mr. Cetina, to find an English version of the document because we have some technical problems. And can you see this document from your crime police department written to the 72nd Battalion before that response you gave to Mr. Cermak, requesting the identification of persons suspected of being involved in one of the previous incidents? Do you identify that as a letter from your crime police department?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this document be exhibited, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1765.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can go now to 65 ter 2D00774.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 18th of September from the crime police department of the police station in Knin under Zadar-Knin Police Administration. And it's an on-site investigation report, containing the date of the 18th of September, compiled on behalf of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We can see during the on-site investigation the official established the following: The fact of the investigation at the Dokici hamlet; the site was not secured and has changed because a number of people and vehicles passed along the street during the course of the night and day; reference to empty bullet shells; photographs by technicians; and time of completion. Is that a correct on-site investigation report from the crime police department at Knin police station?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, might this be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1766.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we could go now to 2D00773.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: From Zadar-Knin Police Administration, 7th Police Station, Knin. 14th of November, 1995. A document to the municipal public prosecutor in Zadar. Criminal report against an unknown perpetrator concerning Simo Dokic, whom we've seen in the original letter from Carmen Burger. And then giving details of what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We see documents that were attached, including that notification of the identity of military personnel of the 72nd Battalion that was sent to the military police of the Knin Company. And we see this was sent by Mr. Gambiroza, the commander of the Knin police station. Is this a correct procedure of a criminal report?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a complete and regular procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At this stage, of course, Knin police station was under the Zadar-Knin Police Administration, rather than the Kotar-Knin Police Administration; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this document be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1767.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, in this procedure, which originated from the letter of Carmen Burger that was passed on to you by -- by General Cermak, beyond that passing on of the information, did General Cermak have any role to play in relation to this case or any of the other cases that were listed within the letter? Any official role?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did he have any unofficial role, any role that was outside the system, whereby he was in any way part of the process?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. When Mr. Cermak sent a letter such as that to you, was he giving you a task? And by a "task," I mean a specific -- a command?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have any obligation to report back to him? We see your letter concerning the information about the cases. Did you have any obligation to send that to him?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The purpose of sending that to him in the letter that you sent was for what reason?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just to inform him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you yourself have meetings with the lady, Carmen Burger, of the International Committee of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You described having meetings with -- or your police administration and you having meetings with UNCIVPOL. Was the Red Cross involved with those UNCIVPOL meetings in any way?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to those cases within Carmen Burger's letter that was sent on to you, could Mr. Cermak order you to investigate those ten or so cases?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In passing on that information, is -- is Mr. Cermak fulfilling any sort of duty or role under the Law on Criminal Procedure of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding the law, he enjoyed the same status as an ordinary citizen would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And are you familiar with Article 142 of the Law of Criminal Procedure of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what does that say?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says - at least as far as I can recall - that all information about crimes should be forwarded by citizens, and institutions are obliged to advise the competent authorities. That is to say, the state prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could just have a look that on the screen. Oh, D1568, Exhibit D1568. Page 3 in the translation. We have extracts. If we could have it in the -- is it possible to get it in the Croatian on the screens? Page 31 in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it's in subclause (1): "If there are reasonable grounds to suspect that a crime which is prosecuted ex officio has been committed. Internal affairs organs shall be required to take the necessary measures to find the perpetrator." And we see the rest of it: to detect, et cetera, gather all information which may be of use for the successful conduct of criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I haven't read it all out there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what General Cermak was doing there, passing on information to you, does that then cause the police to be in the position of being able to suspect that a crime has been committed?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Keeping, in the Croatian, section 140 there, but going back in the English one page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Article 140: "In order to uphold social self-protection, citizens should report crimes which are prosecuted ex officio." Is that the duty, then, that you were referring to, civilians, or people, having the duty to pass on information about crimes?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can go now to P2650.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document that was shown to you and about which you were asked questions. It's dated the 11th of October, 1995. And we see the place Bijelina. And we see the names Dragomir Cotra, Obrad Opacic, someone else Opacic; and the scene of the crime was investigated by an investigating judge; three cartridge cases were found; autopsies established and gun-shot wounds in the head. And that is signed by you. And this was sent to General Cermak. Do you recollect being asked questions about that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you recollect why this letter was written to General Cermak with this information within it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot. But it is possible that it was due to a request from an international institution. But I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Would there be any other reason why you would be informing General Cermak about a particular crime scene?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would writing a letter like this be part of any official procedure of reporting?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you appreciate at the time that the international organisations were putting great pressure on General Cermak for information --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- and results.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- I object to that question. That's leading. And this is not a matter that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't heard the question yet, to be quite honest. Mr. Kay started asking about awareness. Was that your question, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will put it even clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know that the international community were putting great pressure on General Cermak for information, if he could help them provide it, concerning particular crimes?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: He has already answered, Mr. President. My point was that, for one thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MS. MAHINDARATNE -- it was previously leading, but then the second thing, that it doesn't arise from questions asked during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, it certainly does because look, let's be frank about this, this single letter here has been helped up as some kind of reporting procedure of the police to Mr. Cermak, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How closely it relates to it. Let's -- is this a matter of great dispute, first of all, whether the international community was -- was seeking information from Mr. Cermak? I mean, whether you, then, should use the word "pressure" or not is another matter. Is that in dispute, Ms. Mahindaratne?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, we are asking the witness about his knowledge of a fact which is in itself not in dispute. So let's see, then, what the follow-up questions are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, and to be frank, Your Honour, this one document - and I was looking very carefully at the questions by my learned friend, anticipating in several months' time how this could be a phrased in the context of a final brief - and the word "tasks" was being used, "reports." All these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Kay, and let's see what your next question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Let's now go to 2D00784.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is from the crime police department of the Zadar-Knin Police Administration. A criminal report had been filed on the 14th of October. And between the 20th of September and 1st of October an unidentified perpetrator, or perpetrators, had committed a crime - the crime of murder, in fact - against two unidentified men, one woman, in Bijelina; details are given. And on the 10th of October, an on-site investigation had taken place with members of the crime police and the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: External examination. We see what the pathologist discovered and that members of the police administration are investigating. The matter is signed by Mr. Kardum. Just so it's clear, has Mr. Cermak got any role to play in relation to this crime investigation and its procedure at all?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So is the letter of the 11th of October any form of official document within the criminal procedure?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And so did you have to send this document to him, if he had supplied you with any information about the crime?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And are you able to say what the purpose of writing him such a letter would have been?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make this document an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1768.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have here a whole file on this matter, which we would bar table, giving the details of the investigation with photographs. No purpose would be served, I anticipate, in going through this. It's something that my team have found, and we will send it to the Prosecution and bar table it, and in the fullness of time, hopefully it will come before Your Honours. If that meets the Court's approval in dealing with this matter at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay, that's fine. As far as the Chamber is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, it is untranslated material, but since it was a -- a matter raised, it is an incident, and it may be of interest to the Court. We will submit it for translation, and I think that may -- unless the OTP have a copy of these documents translated already, I don't know. But I just inform the Court about that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just one other area I want to ask you questions about. And that concerns this meeting in Plitvice on the 15th of September at the Hotel Jezera, and members of the Ministry of Interior military police were there. What was the purpose of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of the meeting was, together with the heads of the military police, departments of the ministry, and heads of the departments of the Ministry of Interior, to agree on how to act jointly in the relevant area, given that the -- their cooperation up to that point had not been satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were asked questions about that. But at this meeting, did anyone from any of the groups of the military police, Ministry of Interior ever say, Well, to sort out law and order in this area, it's General Cermak you've got to speak to. He's the man who can control it. Did anyone ever suggest General Cermak as being someone who could deal with this?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did anyone ever suggest that General Cermak should deal with this?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did anyone suggest that it was General Cermak's responsibility to deal with this?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Aside of Plitvice, in all the other meetings that you had - and we've seen in various documents some of them - did anyone ever suggest that it was General Cermak's responsibility to deal with these crimes that were happening?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did anyone ever suggest that General Cermak should deal with these crimes that were happening, at any of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There's one other document I'd like to you look at, please. You were asked questions about freedom of movement, and questions were asked about a document, D499. We don't have to have that on the screen. And it was put to you: "If the civilian police were not involved in restricting the movement of monitors, why would Mr. Moric have issued an order?" And it that's document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we look at 65 ter 4420, please. This is the Prosecution 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's dated 8th of August, 1995. It's from Mr. Moric to the police administrations saying Zadar-Knin doesn't include Kotar-Knin. And its subject is: "Arrival of reporters and public figures in the liberated area." And the first part of the order concerns reporters without necessary permissions in the area of Petrinja and Plitvice Lakes, but permission from the Ministry of Defence and Ministry of Interior is needed for other liberated areas. And in paragraph 2 of the order it refers: "When distinguished and generally known public persons enter the liberated area, you must consult the duty operations of the Ministry of Interior Operation Return staff, and for all other persons, access to the liberated area is prohibited until further notice." Do you recollect this particular order?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in relation to this order, what did you -- you do?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were duty-bound to forward it down to the lower-level police units. That's to say, the police stations. And that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No mention here of UNCRO, or the ECMM, or other international organisations. Could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was, and our understanding was that this had to do with the individuals who were likely to come to the area, since this was shortly after the operation itself. And that their access was prohibited for reasons of their own safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May this document be made an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1769.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1769 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour I will have a couple of questions. But I'm looking at the clock and thinking of whether maybe it will be more convenient to have a break now and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If it would take more than five minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I also inquire already with you, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'll have 20 minutes or so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 20 minutes. We will first have a break, but I would first like to invite Madam Usher to escort Mr. Cetina out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I have one small issue in relation to the questions that were put to the witness in relation to the Brgud event, where two unidentified ladies were found. D1753 was put to the witness; that is, a report in which it's stated that a -- information was received about two bodies, that a police car was sent there, that they had not found any bodies, and that a thorough search would be made on the morning of the 13th. And this is all dated the 12th. Now, I asked the witness about any reason why these bodies could not be found, because in P261 we see that on the 13th, in the late afternoon, that the presence of these bodies is again reported - not, this time, by UNCRO - but -- and then you say well, look at -- I have some documents in my -- in the documents I intend to bar table and then you did that immediately, D1757 and D1758, the one being a crime report and the other report on an inside investigation. Now, I take it that the whole exercise from both sides is to thoroughly explore how serious information was dealt with and how adequate police investigations were done. What is missing, in my attempt to get a full picture of what happened, is the morning of the 13th, because we see on the 12th bodies are there, send a police car, cannot find any bodies, but we'll thoroughly investigate the terrain tomorrow morning. And then on the -- by the end of the 13th, it is reported that two bodies are there. And then on the 14th we get the on-site investigation. One of the missing parts in this story is what may have happened on the morning of the 13th, what the results of the announced thorough investigation in the terrain would have been, which, of course, also may have some relevance in how quickly one responded, was one -- information sufficient to take it very seriously or would one wait until the second one? That, apparently, is the issue the parties are struggling with or with disputing about. Is there any information about what happened on the morning of the 13th, which might complete the picture?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've said on several occasions we attempt to put together everything we can, and I think that the Court must appreciate that we are dealing with incomplete records, generally, in this case. To expect, as one would in one's own jurisdiction if one was dealing with a case current this year, that the whole documentary trail is alive and present is simply not possible in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not blaming you for not having it. But what I'm telling you is that -- that we seriously looked at the evidentiary -- the documentary evidentiary material, as we have it now, and that there is something missing. And I'm just inquiring in whether -- that morning of the 13th, whether there is any material that could fill in what seems to be, at least in time, a gap.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I didn't take it any further with this witness because it's to the crime police department. I anticipated the answers would be given. And the witness, dealing, who could have dealt with this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would not primarily expect the witness to tell us anything about it, because he already said that he was guessing --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- why on the 12th they could not find the bodies in familiarity with the terrain. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will have our database examined to see if we can find any material to close that gap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because if it's -- it may be clear to the parties that if it comes to an assessment or a judgement on the adequacy of responses, that details often are important. We'll have a break, and we will resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have had a chance in the break with respect to your last question about that incident, and we have located an Official Note on the 13th concerning all the measures they took. We will have that translated and submitted to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that assists because it completes the picture. Thank you very much for your assistance, Mr. Misetic. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: With your permission, Your Honour, we change our order of our re-cross, so I will go first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Don't make a lot of fuss about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Mikulicic:

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, the basic task of the police in the territory of the Republic of Croatia was regulated by the Law on the Interior. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For ease of reference, it is the Law on Internal Affairs, which was admitted and is now D1077. So as not to waste any Court time, I will simply refer to two articles of that Article -- of that law. In Article 21 of that law, it is stated that, within the ministry, organisational units of are being set up to carry out policing tasks. And these specific organisations were to be called police administration. Is it correct, Mr. Cetina - is it not? - that, under the law, there was a uniformed system of police administrations covering the territory of the Republic of Croatia with the same authorities and duties under the law. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: By virtue of Article 24 of that law, for special security reasons, in order to keep law and order, or in cases of natural disasters and outbreaks of disease, special units of the Ministry of Interior were to be established. Mr. Cetina, I know that in Croatia, back home, laws are changed frequently and it is difficult to keep track sometimes. But I will remind that you the basic Law on the Interior was later on amended by the Law on Amendments to the Law of the Interior which has been made an exhibit. And the number is P1148. By virtue of that law, the duties and role of the special police were clearly prescribed. And I want to ask you about your -- the extent of your knowledge about that. In Article 11 of the law, which is Exhibit P1148, it is stated that it is to combat all types of sabotage and terrorist activities in order to prevent hijacking of vehicles and kidnapping of persons as well as to release hostages and perform other duties which fall within the remit of the ministry under "special conditions." It is for that reason that the special police is being established?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, may I ask, is there any dispute as to the law in force at that time?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No dispute about that. Then what could we expect specifically from this witness? Can he add something, or is it because -- until now it's a bit unclear to me what --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will go further on, and that was only introduction in my next set of questioning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we will wait and here your next questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the Registrar to display Exhibit D1084. Mr. Cetina, while we're waiting for the document, my learned friend from the Prosecution asked you about your authority as the chief of the police administration in relation to the special police unit that was within the police administration itself. And you provided an explanation. I am about to show you a document which the then-minister, Mr. Ivan Vekic, sent as an order to all police administrations, including, I presume, the police administration of Zadar, where, in 1995, you became chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So if I may ask the Registrar, please, D1084. Do we have some technical problems with our e-court? Now it is -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cetina, let me ask you this first. Have you had occasion to see this order in the archives of the Zadar Police Administration when you assumed your position in 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention at paragraph 1, whereby it is ordered that in each police administration a special police unit ought to be formed. Next, paragraph 7, reads: "Special units are to be engaged solely pursuant to decisions issued by the chief of a police administration, and deputy minister of the interior, or the person thus authorised by him." Was this theory translated into practice in keeping with this order?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go to the next page of the document, I'd like to direct your attention at item 8, where it says: "Before engaging a special unit in the area of his administration, the chief of a police administration must obtain clearance from deputy minister or the person authorised by the deputy minister." Does the text of the order tally with the practice you encountered in the performance of your duties?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Next, let's look at item 9 of the document. It is stated: "A special unit cannot be used in the territory of another police administration without a decision of the deputy minister or a person thus designated by him." This was also implemented, was it not?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Cinci -- I apologise. Mr. Cetina, such a practice was in place in peacetime conditions, rather than in situations in which the special police force was used as part of war operations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, I have just called you Mr. Cinci a minute ago. Hence my question is whether you now Mr. Cinci, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He was the chief of the Split Police Administration while you were the chief of the Zadar Police Administration; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is your impression of Mr. Cinci that of a professional, of a person who performed his duties professionally?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will quote to you a portion of his statement he gave before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is Exhibit D1723.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have that on the screen. Otherwise, I'll simply read out the portion I'm interested in and then I'll ask for your comment. Mr. Cinci says as follows in paragraph 2 at page 2 of his statement: "The minister of the interior of the Republic of Croatia was, in terms of territory, split between police administrations and, professionally speaking, by sectors. There was a sector for the regular police, crime police, special police, finance, civil protection, and other sectors." The police administrations also consisted of sectors for basic crime investigation, special police, and then I will skip a portion. "And they were run by chiefs of sectors. The chiefs of sectors within the police administration were, at the same time, responsible to the PA chiefs and, according to the professional line, to the assistant ministers for their sector?" Do you agree with this interpretation? Is it the way you see the organisation of the ministry?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, I'll draw your attention next to paragraph 3 where Mr. Cinci says as follows: "The exception was the special police, which, because of the specific nature of their tasks, had different lines of subordination, depending on the situation. For instance, in the special police sector of my police administration, there were about 200 policemen. When they were in Split, in my area of responsibility, the special police commander was responsible exclusively to me as a police administration chief. But, when they participated in joint actions of the special police from several police administrations, they were under the command of Mr. Mladen Markac, assistant minister, and Zeljko Sacic, special police sector chief. "However, when the special police members participated in military police operations, of which there were many, Mr. Markac was responsible to the Main Staff chief of the Croatian Army. At that moment, Mr. Markac, regardless of the fact that he was assistant minister of the interior, was not responsible to Minister Jarnjak, and he did not have to report to him on anything." Mr. Cetina do you agree with that with this description as given by your colleague, Mr. Cipci?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us move on to another topic which will my last, Mr. Cetina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For that purpose, I would like to ask the Registrar to display D179.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, you're a professional, a career policeman. By the way, how long have you been performing police duties in the various forms?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 25 years now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the course of your duties as the chief of the Zadar Police Administration, you had occasion to meet Mr. Jan Elleby, who was the chief of the CIVPOL in Sector South; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you get -- any information or did you gain an impression of -- about how long he had performed police duties by the time when you acted as the chief of the Zadar Police Administration?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, Mr. Cetina: As a career policeman, based on your professional experience as well as knowledge of the regulations which defined your remit and official terminology, in official correspondence and communication, did you ever pay attention to the use of terminology you used to describe the events which fell under your competence?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you believe it to be an important part of police work and the performance of police duties?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, before you is a document you were shown a few days ago. It was sent to you by Mr. Jan Elleby. The title of which is: "List of murders committed since the 4th of August 1995." Do you understand any death to fall under the category of murder or does it entail something else? And, if so, please tell us what.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A murder only took place if a person was killed -- if the person suffered a violent death.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Does that entail suspicion of a crime?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to establish grounds for suspicion, one needs to carry out certain activities, in keeping with the Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the Registrar to move to the next page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: To repeat, Mr. Elleby titled this document: "List of murders." Let us look at paragraph 4 of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, this Chamber is more or less aware of the legal definition of murder. The Chamber is also aware that Mr. Elleby used the word "murders" on the cover page. What are we exploring at this moment? Whether Mr. Elleby, in view of what we see in the document, on the basis of that alone, could not qualify all of the events as murder, so, therefore, he has been imprecise in his language? Or are we further exploring -- I mean, some matters seem to be rather obvious -- if you find two bodies and whether they're murdered or not, often it does not follow from the description. That's obvious even without any further questions put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is anything else you would like to draw our attention to, please feel free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm grateful for such position of the Trial Chamber. I would like just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not a position. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour, in fact. I will just like to stress the Chamber's attention that paragraph 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 12, 13, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 22, 28, and 32 has qualifications that one could not undertake under the term of "murder." And that was my point. And I would like do ask the witness only one question on that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's be quite clear, since you're talking about the position of the Chamber. The way in which the events are described here would not be sufficient to qualify them as murders, that's more or less -- that's a legal issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether Mr. Elleby had any other reasons, for example, reports sent to him, to put these events in his list, is, of course, a totally different matter. I think we would agree on that. Isn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For example - and I'm not further focussing on Brgud, but - if you look at the other documentation, there may be reasons to believe that there was intention of killing of the two unidentified ladies. Still not known by whom. Not sufficient to -- perhaps to qualify it as a murder. But you need more information than what we find in this document to qualify these events as murder events. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Then, please put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's clear. Especially when, for example, in paragraph 4, well, the event has been previously described as a murder. It is stated that was impossible to a certain age or cause of death. So it is a bit of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, at least --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... the one. I don't know whether, at any later stage, it had been possible to establish age and cause of death. But at least, from this document, nothing appears which would qualify number 4 as a murder. But it's rather a decomposed corpse found. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cetina, a question regarding this document. When you received it, did you continue your discussions with Mr. Elleby, concerning these -- qualification of these offences and murder, although they're not supported in the allegations contained in the document? Did you continue your discussions with him on this?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question, Mr. Cetina. During your tenure as the chief of the Zadar Police Administration, you went through an eventful period; there were a great many activities in the area of responsibility of area police administration. Had anyone ever, in relation to you or as far as you know in relation to your associates, excerpt any sort of pressures along the lines that you should not be adhering to the law or that you should tolerate crime? Were you ever a witness to any such actions?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Further cross-examination by Mr. Misetic:

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, you were asked a few questions about Kistanje, and I would like to ask you a few questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have on the screen, please, Exhibit D1326, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, what will come up on the screen is -- should be an assessment of the number of burned houses in Kistanje. It's based on statistics provided by the UN Military Observers, or UNMOs, from a report they prepared on 4th of November, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's D1326.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, we have the English on the screen. Hopefully, you will be able to follow it. In the upper right-hand corner are statistics from the 1991 census about the total population, and then in blue you will see a number for the total number of buildings in the village of Kistanje area, according to the 1991 census. And the number on the census was 547. You will see on the map all of the various hamlets that make up Kistanje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then if we could turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Then on this chart all of the hamlets that were identified by UNMO as having been inspected by UNMO from the village of Kistanje are included here. And can you see the totals at the bottom, that UNMO found, as of 4th of November, 101 totally destroyed buildings and 63 partially destroyed buildings. Now, these statistics would suggest that there were 101 out of a possible 547 totally destroyed buildings in Kistanje as of the 4th of November, 1995. You were asked in cross-examination whether the majority of buildings in Kistanje were destroyed as of, approximately, I believe, the date was 14th of August, that was given to you. My question to you is: Did you actually do your own inspection of the Kistanje area to check to see how many houses had been destroyed, how many partially destroyed, and how many, in fact, weren't destroyed at all?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Okay. When you told the Presiding Judge that the majority of houses were destroyed as of the 14th of August, what was -- what was that based on? What did you base that observation on?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on what I was able to observe as I was passing through the centre of the settlement. And from what I recall of the houses I saw, quite a few were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Okay. The centre of Kistanje, give us an approximation. How many houses are in the centre -- I should say how many buildings are in the centre of Kistanje, from your recollection?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. But that was the first time I visited the area. I think that I, in fact, passed along one street only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, can you give us an approximation? Is there -- would you say there were 200 houses in the centre --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the witness has answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't disallow Mr. Misetic to a bit further explore, although there is also some risk of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm just trying to understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Trying to relate the concept of what it means when you say the majority of houses. I'm trying to relate that specifically to some figures. Can you give us a ballpark estimate of how many houses, to the best of your recollection, and I'm not asking you to be precise, but to the best of your recollection, in the centre of Kistanje, how many buildings are there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Truly, I didn't count the houses and buildings. I really don't have an idea of the width of the settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber has heard evidence from the head of the human rights monitoring teams in Sector South that he was in Kistanje on the 13th of August and counted seven houses burned in the centre of Kistanje. Is that consistent or is that roughly --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I had --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- coincide with your recollections?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to this. The witness has clearly answered that he is unable to give any estimate at all, even a ballpark figure. He has been very precise. And to then explore this further and to put to the witness other figures given by witnesses is not appropriate, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I tend to agree. There's nothing opposed against -- there's nothing against asking the witness do seek whether he has any further information. But until now, all his answers went in the same direction and that is that he had only limited view on the matter. And then to put all kind of different estimates and to try to find out which he likes most is perhaps not the way we should proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't mind, Mr. President, but I'm just -- in anticipation of an argument later that the witness said "totally destroyed" or "majority destroyed." As long as we're clear that -- I attempted to get a more specific number as to what that really means and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What we know is that the witness told us that he doesn't know exactly where the boundaries of Kistanje are, that he drove through the centre, and that when he uses the word "majority" that that might be influenced by his limited sight of -- of the location. That --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- seems to be the core. And then, of course, we have to evaluate the evidence of this witness, together with all the other evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have Exhibit D915, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, I'm going to show you an Official Note of a interview of Mr. Zvonimir Lasan in the course of the Varivode investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 4 in the Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, I would turn your attention to that first paragraph in the Croatian towards the bottom. And the last sentence Mr. Lasan, in his police interview, said: "Aside from this murder, Zvonimir states that he didn't kill or shoot at anyone else after Operation Storm, besides shooting at some Chetniks during the operation and burning one house when they enter Kistanje, which he thought was a Chetnik house because he saw a lot of books there that were mostly in Cyrillic and a picture of a man in a Yugoslav uniform." Now, my question to you is: When Mr. Lasan acknowledged at least setting one house on fire in Kistanje during Operation Storm, did the police open a further investigation into Mr. Lasan and his associates who were then being suspected of the Varivode murders to see what else they may have done in Kistanje during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. These are the details of a case in which the criminal investigation police was engaged, and I don't remember what steps were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, would you agree with me, on the basis of this Official Note, there at least was some information available to the police as to who it might have been involved in setting fire to houses during Operation Storm in Kistanje?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention now to this issue of MUP acting towards HV members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if could I have Exhibit D57 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will try to show you several examples, Mr. Cetina. This is the Knin police station log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could go first to English page 43 and Croatian page 43, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Looking at the first entry, number 147, the police report that they stopped a passenger vehicle with members of the Croatian army who were transporting different household appliances. And the course of action taken is the duty officer of the 72nd Military Police Battalion Sergeant 1st Class, Knezic [phoen], who took over the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn to English page 72, Croatian page 76.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is entry number 223. This is the 29th of August. The police car patrol brought from the Krka check-point three persons in a passenger car. It goes on to say that -- towards the bottom, they were wearing Croatian army uniforms, although they are not members of the Croatian army. Course of action taken is they were handed over to the crime police officer who confiscated the goods from them and issued a relevant receipt. These three persons left the premises of the first police station at 2200 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The next entry is at page 86 in the English, page 93 in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is entry 248. On the 2nd of September, at 1210 hours, at the police station Kistanje, the duty officer reported that their officers had stopped two HV personnel and one MUP personnel who were transporting items. Then there's the course of action that they took against the two HV and one police officer who were in this car. Mr. Cetina, I won't take more time, but I will tell you that there's well over a dozen such examples of -- in this log-book alone of police taking action against either persons who were confirmed to be members of the HV or were wearing Croatian army uniforms and the police took action against them. And if I could show you one additional exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is Exhibit D486, please. And this will be ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is under seal, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now this is a report, Mr. Cetina, about an incident that took place on the 19th of September. And if you read through it, it talks about this incident taking place at a check-point. "The car had no registration plates. When the officials Mladen Zuteg [phoen] and Arsen Stefanic [phoen] pulled over the car, the co-driver," and then it gives the HV member's military police post address, "pulled over the car, the co-driver, Miroslav Lucin [phoen], came into oral conflict with the aforementioned policemen, offending them, and preventing them in exercising their duty. Then he sat in the driver's seat aiming to drive away. The policeman Arsen Stefanic fired two rounds of ammunition from a machine-gun in the rear left car tire to prevent him to drive away. "The officials in the 6th Police Station Benkovac and 72nd Battalion of the Military Police Benkovac operated on the site. Miroslav Lucin was brought into the premises of the 72nd MPs," et cetera. And I can tell you, the Chamber has Exhibit D842, which is the military police's report of this incident. And that report shows that, in fact, the military police were not at this check-point when the shots were fired by the policemen to stop the car. They were only called in after the HV member was detained. Mr. Cetina, looking at this material, would you agree with me that, while officers may have been afraid in certain circumstances to take action, there were, in fact, numerous occasions when your police officers, in fact, did take action against persons in military uniforms, whether they were in the HV formally or not?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, I would like to show you three final documents, and this has to do with the issue of sanitation of the terrain and whether there were investigations carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could have Exhibit D1396 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were asked questions by the Prosecution concerning a meeting on the 6th of August in which there was a discussion about -- in the sanitation of terrain there -- operative investigations did not have to be conducted. You testified that you weren't aware of that conversation. And I'd like to show you three on-site investigations. This is from the 11th of August; it's from the Sibenik Police Administration. If you look towards the bottom it says, under point 1: "The on-site investigation is conducted based on information received from an unknown member of the 142nd Brigade." At the top, it says the date of commission is 6 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You'll see, under point 6, an on-site investigation, in fact, was carried out. And if we look through that, can you see the results of the on-site investigation. In the interests of time, Mr. Cetina, I will tell you that there at least two other such on-site investigations for bodies found prior to the 10th of August, and those are D1397 and D1398. My question to you, Mr. Cetina, is: In fact, it was up to the sanitation teams -- let me rephrase that. In fact, investigations of bodies found did go on immediately after Operation Storm, as far as you know, if circumstances dictated that there was a suspicion that something of a criminal nature may have taken place. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cetina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have in further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just for clarity of the record, Mr. Misetic mentioned the discussion with regard to the sanitation issue and that was not 6th August. 7th August. I just wished to point that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was trying to find it, as a matter of fact, but I couldn't find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, Judge Kinis has one or more questions for you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, Judge Kinis has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, I would like to -- referring back to Exhibit D598. This is a report, Tomurad to Josko Moric. Could you please bring up on the screen, this document. Second page, please. No, this is not ... I'm sorry, this is not the right one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 589, I think, is the document Your Honour requires.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: 589, yes. Yeah. 589, yes. In the second page of this document there is mentioned -- Mr. Tomurad mentions that there are such situations that individuals who are taking away property on basis of written permissions issued by municipal presidents. My question is: If such actions did take place, and obviously it was, what kind of measures was prepared in order to stop such? And was there some -- some activities -- or some actions to -- to call such persons to criminal liability?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These certificates or permissions were not considered valid by the police, and in such cases, the objects concerned were to be confiscated or seized.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: And there was no action taken against those persons who issued such certificates?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I remember, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: And the next question is regarding restrictions of UNCIVPOL. Witness Laila Malm, from UNCIVPOL, testified on the 11th September, 1995; she visited Gracac graveyard. And after a couple of minutes, a Croatian police officer arrived and told witness to left -- leave this graveyard. Could you comment on this, please.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He -- it is highly likely that he did not the relevant documentation that would have permitted him to gain access to the graveyard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: What kind of documentation UNCIVPOL officer should get? You are referring documentation, what kind of documentation you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I wanted to say, that the police officer did not have an order from his superior to prevent visits from taking place, visits to the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: But it happened. We received numerous evidence on this. And finally, Ms. Prosecutor asked this question regarding the determination of dead bodies, particularly who was a victim of combat and who was a victim of murder. And could you please explain whether such a criteria include area or time-limits or characters of wounds, or maybe some other characteristics, where policemen or persons who will deal with these matters immediately can decide that there is no necessity for on-site investigation and just send sanitation teams, which actually happens on the ground.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The persons who were out in the field always have most information and are always better placed to decide on what needed to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: But we received numerous evidence, including these entries into Knin log-book, police log-book, where policemen, immediately after they receiving information about dead bodies was found, immediately informed just sanitation team and that's all. No -- any actions were taken.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a procedure that was worked out by the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: But you mentioned that -- you mentioned all time and you reiterate many times that law has supremacy over orders issued by officials of ministry.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Where there are reasonable doubts for suspicion that a crime was committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Actually, it does not answer my question. But thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, one follow-up question on a matter which was raised in relation to your involvement in mop-up operations of the special police. You said you were not involved in organising or planning. You may have been informed. Were you asked, assistance of a limited nature, such as, keep civilians out of that area or keep others out of that area when there -- when a mop-up operation was planned?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that I received some notification. But as for detailed plans of engagement of the police, that is something I was not privy to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I didn't ask you whether you were privy of detailed plans. I asked you whether, when you were notified, whether it was expected that you would assist, although perhaps in a very limited way, and I gave a possible example of keeping out civilians of the area where the mop-up operation would take place. So let's stop civilians to go to Village A, B, and C, because there will be a mop-up operation. And this is just an example. I'm asking you whether any kind of assistance was asked from you or required from you or whether you even were ordered to give such assistance.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive such an order. It is possible that a notification was sent, and if the regular police, indeed, participated, it was probably along the roads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I asked you about whether you were asked, whether you were requested, whether you were ordered, and in your answer you limited to that you never received such an order. And you say: "It is possible that the regular police, indeed, participated ... along the roads." Could you give us a bit more information about such participation. Who would ask you to do that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: An order is an order to me. If I'm instructed to do something, I do. On the other hand, we may have received some information of police activity in the broader area. And if we assessed that it was necessary to stop people moving along roads from getting off and getting into the area in order to keep them safe, then we tried to keep them out of such areas of combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you were, from what I understand, notified as to when and where; and then, if you considered it useful to take any action in order to guarantee safety, you would take action?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us one example? And could you also tell us how many of your men were then involved?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there were such instances, they happened seldom. Such information was forwarded, usually, to the chief of the police station involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking you whether you could give us an example.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA [Resumed]
